3.1.2. Data on EPA Regulatory Activities. Our data on the EPA’s enforce- ment, monitoring, and rulemaking activities are compiled from various sources. First, we collect information on EPA enforcement cases from the Federal Enforcement and Compliance (FE&C) files maintained by the

EPA’s Integrated Compliance Information System (ICIS). As the official repository for environmental compliance records, the ICIS tracks all for- mal enforcement and monitoring activities led by the EPA. For each en- forcement case, the FE&C files contain (1) general case-level information (e.g., case number, case type, case milestone dates), (2) firm-facility in- formation (e.g., defendant firms, violating facilities), (3) violation details (e.g., pollution type, violated law/statute), and (4) enforcement decisions (e.g., compliance cost, monetary penalty). Second, we obtain EPA moni- toring data from the FE&C’s compliance inspection files, which contain both inspection-level information (e.g., inspection type, inspection time, relevant law/statute) and facility information (e.g., facility name and iden- tifier). We aggregate the enforcement and inspection data at the firm level and match those with the Compustat-CRSP merged file based on company names.11 Lastly, we collect data on the EPA’s rulemaking activities from the Federal Register website, which provides comprehensive coverage of

final order documents from the EPA’s website.15 Among the 865 cases un- der consideration, 272 have corresponding final order documents. From these documents, we collect information about the discovery dates of the underlying violations. In particular, we identify the specific discovery dates in 223 out of the 272 final orders and use the month subsequent to the last discovery date as the beginning of the investigation stage. The end of the investigation stage is defined as the month immediately preceding the case resolution (i.e., the final order date), which is available for all 865 cases in our sample. We further augment our dataset by extracting discovery dates for 74 additional cases from the FE&C database.

data_section_full_text:
3. Data and Descriptive Statistics
3.1 data
  3.1.1. Data on EPA Downloads. The EDGAR server log files contain com-
prehensive records of online access to millions of SEC-mandated filings
over the past two decades. These files furnish detailed information, includ-
ing (1) the Central Index Key (CIK) of the requesting firm, (2) the times-
tamp for each request, (3) the IP address of the requesting user, and (4)

the accession number uniquely identifying each filing or form. For privacy
reasons, the final octet of the IP address is anonymized and replaced with
a distinctive set of three letters. To track the EPA’s requests via EDGAR, we
use “WHOIS” and “WHOWAS” query tools supported by the American Reg-
istry for Internet Numbers to identify various IP blocks owned by the EPA.
This approach enables us to identify the EPA’s queries even with partially
anonymized IP addresses.10
   The EDGAR server log files offer several valuable features for our re-
search goals. First, the dataset records all the “clicks” made by the EPA to
request firm-specific SEC filings through the EDGAR system. Second, the
exact timing of each click is recorded, allowing us to determine when the
EPA retrieved a firm’s SEC filings. This is crucial for establishing a direct
link between EPA downloads and its regulatory activities, a connection we
explore using an event-study design (see section 4.1.1). Third, from the log
files, we can observe which SEC filings were requested by the EPA, enabling
us to infer the relative importance of different reports for regulatory pur-
poses. These features allow us to effectively capture the EPA’s acquisition
and utilization of firm-specific EDGAR filings. Additionally, our empirical
approach aligns with recent studies that measure downloads of SEC filings
by the IRS, the Fed, and the SEC (e.g., Bozanic et al. [2017], Fox and Wil-
son [2023], Guo and Tian [2023], Li et al. [2023], Holzman, Marshall, and
Schmidt [2024], Iselin et al. [2024]). Unlike those studies, however, our
focus is on the EPA—a critical regulatory entity that concentrates on envi-
ronmental protection and human health.
   Upon gathering all records associated with the EPA’s IP blocks, we aggre-
gate each firm’s EPA downloads on a monthly basis and match the data with
the Compustat-CRSP merged file using CIK codes. Following prior research
(e.g., Guo and Tian [2023], Li et al. [2023]), we construct two measures of
EPA downloads. The first measure, DOWNLOAD, is an indicator variable
taking the value of one if a firm is the subject of at least one EPA download
in the current month and zero otherwise. The second measure, DLFREQ,
quantifies the frequency of EPA downloads of a firm’s SEC filings within
a given month. Consequently, these measures capture EPA downloads in
terms of both probability and frequency. Consistent with the extant litera-
ture (e.g., Fox and Wilson [2023], Guo and Tian [2023]), our choice of a
monthly window enables us to attribute changes in EPA downloads to its
regulatory events.
  3.1.2. Data on EPA Regulatory Activities. Our data on the EPA’s enforce-
ment, monitoring, and rulemaking activities are compiled from various
sources. First, we collect information on EPA enforcement cases from the
Federal Enforcement and Compliance (FE&C) files maintained by the


   10 For example, one of the IP blocks owned by the EPA is 134.67.0.0–134.67.255.255. Consis-

tent with the literature (e.g., Lee, Ma, and Wang [2015], Bozanic et al. [2017]), our measure
of EPA downloads is based on IP version 4 (IPv4).

EPA’s Integrated Compliance Information System (ICIS). As the official
repository for environmental compliance records, the ICIS tracks all for-
mal enforcement and monitoring activities led by the EPA. For each en-
forcement case, the FE&C files contain (1) general case-level information
(e.g., case number, case type, case milestone dates), (2) firm-facility in-
formation (e.g., defendant firms, violating facilities), (3) violation details
(e.g., pollution type, violated law/statute), and (4) enforcement decisions
(e.g., compliance cost, monetary penalty). Second, we obtain EPA moni-
toring data from the FE&C’s compliance inspection files, which contain
both inspection-level information (e.g., inspection type, inspection time,
relevant law/statute) and facility information (e.g., facility name and iden-
tifier). We aggregate the enforcement and inspection data at the firm level
and match those with the Compustat-CRSP merged file based on company
names.11 Lastly, we collect data on the EPA’s rulemaking activities from
the Federal Register website, which provides comprehensive coverage of
rulemaking activities by all U.S. federal agencies. Following prior literature
(e.g., Johnson [2008], Kalmenovitz [2023]), we retrieve information on
the timing and content of each “significant” rule (as defined by Executive
Order 12866) proposed by the EPA within our sample period. To identify
firms potentially affected by each rule, we extract details about the affected
industries using the NAICS codes specified in the text of each rule pro-
posal (with different digit levels) and then match the proposed rules with
our sample firms based on industry classifications.
3.2 sample selection
   We begin with all U.S. public firms on the Compustat-CRSP merged
files between January 2003 and June 2017. The beginning and end of our
sample period are determined by the availability of the EDGAR server
log files. To ensure the relevance of the EPA’s regulatory actions for our
sample firms, we remove industries (six-digit NAICS codes) without any
EPA enforcement activities during the entire sample period.12 In addition,
we follow prior research studying EPA data (e.g., Xu and Kim [2022])
and remove firms not listed on NYSE, NASDAQ, or AMEX and those with
missing control variables. Our final sample includes 246,826 firm-month
observations, representing 3,176 unique firms, between January 2003 and
June 2017 (see table 2, panel A).
   Over the 14.5-year period, our sample firms are subject to 865 enforce-
ment cases, 5,257 compliance inspections, and 237 significant rule propos-
als by the EPA (not tabulated). The selection of enforcement cases involves

   11 To ensure a direct link between EPA downloads and enforcement, we remove the cases

that have more than one defendant (parent) firm. Our results are robust to including these
cases, which account for about 8% of the total cases (see table OA1 in the online appendix).
   12 For example, this selection criterion removes the financial industry, which has no record

of enforcement actions during our sample period. Our results are quantitatively and qual-
itatively similar when we retain all industries in the sample (see table OA2 in the online
appendix).

a three-step procedure. First, we gather all cases from the EPA’s FE&C
database with final resolution dates falling within our sample period and
remove noncorporate entities. The second step involves a fuzzy matching
process between the defendants’ company names in the FE&C files and
firm names in the Compustat-CRSP database. Manual data cleaning is then
applied to ensure exact matching. In the final step, these cases are matched
with the final sample, resulting in 865 unique cases for our sample firms.13
   A similar procedure is performed for the selection of compliance inspec-
tions. We collect all EPA inspections from the FE&C files, ensuring that the
inspection dates align with our sample period and excluding noncorporate
entities. We perform fuzzy matching and manual cleaning on the inspec-
tion data. After matching it with the final sample, we identify 5,257 unique
inspections for our sample firms.
   For rule proposals, our selection procedure begins with all EPA doc-
uments obtained from the Federal Register website within our sample
period. We exclude documents related to public hearings and comment
period extensions, retaining only significant rule proposals per Executive
Order 12866. Subsequently, we eliminate rule proposals where the affected
industries cannot be identified and merge the remaining proposals with
the final sample, resulting in 237 unique rules for our sample firms. Note
that, unlike enforcement cases or inspections that individually affect only
a single firm, each significant rule proposal may affect multiple industries
and many firms.

13 See table OA3 in the online appendix for more information about the sample selection

process. When aggregating our sample to the firm-year level (untabulated), about 6.3% are
impacted by the 865 enforcement cases we identified. This aligns with the findings of Xu and
Kim [2022, p. 607], who note that “legal enforcement activities are infrequent in the sample,
with only about 4.3% of the observations undergoing investigations related to environmen-
tal issues.” Additionally, around 9% of the firm-year samples are subject to at least one EPA
inspection, while 85% are influenced by at least one significant rule proposal.

As noted earlier, the EPA resolves each enforcement case by (1) issuing a
final administrative order or (2) transferring the case to the DOJ. Accord-
ingly, the resolution stage is defined as the month in which a final order is
issued (i.e., either a final administrative order or a transfer to the DOJ). To
ascertain the duration of the investigation stage, we download all available

final order documents from the EPA’s website.15 Among the 865 cases un-
der consideration, 272 have corresponding final order documents. From
these documents, we collect information about the discovery dates of the
underlying violations. In particular, we identify the specific discovery dates
in 223 out of the 272 final orders and use the month subsequent to the last
discovery date as the beginning of the investigation stage. The end of the
investigation stage is defined as the month immediately preceding the case
resolution (i.e., the final order date), which is available for all 865 cases in
our sample. We further augment our dataset by extracting discovery dates
for 74 additional cases from the FE&C database.
   For these 297 cases (= 223 + 74), we develop an empirical model to
explain the duration of the investigation periods based on their case char-
acteristics (see appendix III). For all remaining cases, we determine the
investigation period by applying the estimates derived from the empirical
model to their respective case characteristics. For all 865 cases, the average
duration of the investigation stage is about eight months, which is broadly
consistent with the enforcement timeframe outlined in the EPA’s internal
document.16 After ascertaining the investigation period, we define the dis-
covery stage as the six-month period prior to case investigation, and the
review stage as the 12-month period following case resolution.

15 See https://yosemite.epa.gov/oa/rhc/epaadmin.nsf (accessed in November 2023).
